description: We are a Houston team of high school students and college freshmen working on NASA’s “Dancing with the SARs” challenge. We’re interested in coding, AI, engineering, space, and Earth science. We’re looking for teammates skilled in coding, data analysis, design, research, or anyone willing to learn and contribute.
summary: CryoTrace is a public web app that helps people explore how glaciers and the terrain around them change. For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we compared two NASA–ISRO NISAR radar passes over Hubbard Glacier that bracket the December 6, 2025 earthquake. Users can swipe between the images, inspect 143 radar change candidates, and compare them with a preliminary USGS inventory. Each patch shows how much the radar signal changed and how much area it covers. The project also includes a Columbia Glacier Landsat timeline, an atlas of 18 glaciers, and Cryo AI for questions with clickable sources. CryoTrace makes satellite data easier to explore and helps students, educators, and other users evaluate what the observations can tell them.
details:
CryoTrace is an interactive glacier observatory that helps people explore how glaciers change over time using real satellite data. We built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to make radar and optical imagery easier to explore for students, educators, and anyone curious about Earth’s changing ice.

The experience starts with an interactive globe. Visitors can select a glacier, see where it is, and explore the observations available for that location. At Alaska’s Columbia Glacier, visitors can slide between dated NASA and USGS Landsat images to see how the ice front has retreated since 1986. At Hubbard Glacier, they can compare two NISAR radar passes, filter areas by the strength of the radar change, and select individual patches to inspect their measurements. For other glaciers in the radar catalog, visitors can see when NISAR passed over the area and where each scene was captured. Cryo AI lets visitors ask questions about glaciers and provides source links so they can check the evidence themselves.

We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, used Leaflet for interactive maps, and deployed it on Hostinger with a PHP backend that manages the AI connection and keeps the API key server-side. We also included tools for plotting dated glacier front positions, exporting traces as GeoJSON, and charting results from the Open Global Glacier Model (OGGM).

Our creative choice was to let visitors investigate a change themselves. A visitor can start with “What changed here?”, compare the same spot across two dates, and then ask Cryo AI what might explain the difference. We considered how seasonal snow, image alignment, and changes in radar brightness can affect interpretation. CryoTrace labels modeled projections and explains what the imagery can support, so visitors can distinguish a visible change from a possible explanation.
